questions.title: Does a 'reasonable observer' standard apply when determining the 'purpose and character' factor of Fair Use, or does the user's subjective intent matter?
questions.question_body: I'm reading *Santos v. Kimmel*, where the Second Circuit relies on *Andy Warhol Found. Inc. v. Goldsmith* to dismiss Santos's copyright claim. Kimmel argues he instigated the creation of the videos, implying a personal purpose, but the court dismisses this as 'subjective intent.' Why is the objective 'reasonable observer' standard the controlling metric for transformative use in the Second Circuit, and does this show I need to rethink how I apply the first fair use factor in case briefs?

questions.title: Can bad faith or deceptive conduct, like using fictitious names on a service, negate a Fair Use defense?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that Santos's complaint contains depictions of 'Kimmel's false representations' but notes the Supreme Court has 'distanced itself' from *Harper & Row*. However, *Harper & Row* held fair use 'presupposes good faith and fair dealing.' In a real-world litigation scenario, if the mock user used fake identities (Cameo platform), I would think this bad faith should be fatal to the claim. Did the Second Circuit's reasoning here overturn the traditional rule or simply limit the scope of what constitutes bad faith nullifying the defense?

questions.title: How does the Second Circuit apply 'market usurpation' versus 'market devaluation' when deciding Factor 4 (Market Effect)?
questions.question_body: In the fair use discussion, the court distinguishes 'devaluing' the first work through criticism from 'usurping' the market by offering a competing substitute. It quotes *Hachette* saying 'unlikelihood that creators... will license critical reviews... removes such uses from... potential licensing market.' Why does this distinction matter for a quoting satire where the secondary creator explicitly offers a different purpose? Is this relevant when the plaintiff argues the videos might still have commercial value?

questions.title: Why did the Second Circuit avoid resolving the Preemption issue regarding Santos's state law claims?
questions.question_body: Santos argued his contract claims were not preempted by the Copyright Act, whereas the court said they 'failed to state a claim.' The opinion states: 'We need not resolve this issue.' Procedurally, does this suggest that if a state law claim fails under state pleading standards, federal preemption is not a viable path of appeal? If I have a case where preemption is the defense, does failing to plead the contract effectively waive the need to analyze § 301(a) of the Copyright Act?

questions.title: Under what circumstances can a party enforce a Terms of Service against a non-party user via 'express declaration'?
questions.question_body: Santos claims a breach of the Cameo Terms of Service but notes he wasn't a party to it. The court cites *Barry v. St. Mary's Hosp.* and New York law which requires an 'express declaration' to allow non-contracting third parties to benefit. Even though the Terms apply to Kimmel, does the absolute requirement for an 'express declaration' apply strictly when invoking Illinois law or New York law in a contract dispute regarding platform terms? Does this mean users without accounts can rarely sue under ToS?

questions.title: Why does New York law require an allegation of 'out-of-pocket loss' for a fraudulent inducement claim?
questions.question_body: The court dismisses Santos's fraudulent inducement claim because he 'failed to allege that he suffered any actual out-of-pocket loss.' I know fraud generally requires harm, but I thought fraudulent inducement might just need to show reliance plus damages. I am specifically confused if the court is requiring 'out-of-pocket loss' as a distinct element for New York fraudulent inducement, rather than just general compensatory damages or relational damages.

questions.title: How does the pleading standard under Rule 12(b)(6) apply to complex fair use defenses like 'devaluation' vs. 'superseding'?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites *TCA Television Corp.* saying fair use can be 'so clearly established by a complaint as to support dismissal.' Given that fair use factors are flexible and vary by context (*Andy Warhol*, *Hachette*), how does a judge in the 2nd Circuit draw the line between a 'plausibly argued defense' and a claim 'so clearly established' that it bars the suit at the 12(b)(6) stage, especially when market harm is objectively difficult to prove?
